title: The great sayings
hookLine: describe yourself in one sentence: the Upanishads tried
carry: you are that: the self is brahman
tomorrow: a Tamil poem opens with a question, not a blessing. what is it?

lines: FOUR LINES ON A STICKY NOTE.
cards: A scholarship form, a dating profile, a team bio: sooner or later something asks you to describe yourself in one sentence. What comes out is usually a list. Runner.
Coffee person. Big sister. The Upanishads have a handful of one-line answers, short enough for a sticky note and stranger than any profile.
Consciousness is Brahman. I am Brahman. You are that.
This self is Brahman. Advaita calls them the great sayings, mahavakyas, and the Panchadashi gives them a chapter, one word at a time.

teach.b: The book points to the awareness by which a person sees, hears, smells, speaks and tastes. That same awareness, in every creature, it says, is Brahman. Next, I am Brahman.
Here the I isn't the patron from yesterday's theater, the small self that wants the show to be about it. It's the full awareness the book has been pointing to all week.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI, WORD BY WORD.
teach.b: Then the line a father, Uddalaka, says to his son in the Chandogya Upanishad: tat tvam asi, you are that. The Panchadashi slows down. That means the reality there before the world's names and forms.
You means the self behind body and mind. Are joins them. Last, this self is Brahman.
This means near, right here: the self within, shining as the inner witness. Here's something to tell a friend tonight. Read fast, I am Brahman sounds like a brag.

teach.h: THE BRAGGING I IS LOOKED PAST.
teach.b: Read the way this chapter reads it, it's nearly the opposite: the I that brags is exactly the one being looked past.
Other Vedanta schools read these sayings differently, and the Panchadashi gives the Advaita reading plainly.

how: In Advaita teaching the great sayings are heard from a teacher, reflected on, and dwelt on; students often take one saying at a time, word by word.

o: a book of Advaita verses ending with the great sayings
a book of rules for kings and how to rule a land
a book of hymns for lighting the evening lamp

games.q: the great sayings — tap the pairs.
p: the awareness behind seeing and hearing
the reality before names and forms
near, right here, the self within

s: 'I am Brahman' means a person's ego is divine
in the Panchadashi, the I is full awareness, not the ego.
'you are that' is a father's line to his son in the Chandogya Upanishad
Uddalaka to Shvetaketu; the Panchadashi weighs it word by word.
'this self is Brahman' points to something far off in the sky
this means near, right here: the self within.

games.q: your cousin sees 'I am Brahman' on a poster and says it sounds like ego in a nicer font. which I does the chapter mean?
o: the full awareness, not the small self that wants the show.
a confident self that believes in its own success.
the person's name and life story, made holy.
games.why: the Panchadashi looks past the patron, the I that wants the show, to the awareness it's pointed at all week.

practice: If there's a pen nearby, write one honest line about yourself, the kind a form would ask for. Under it, write: who is reading this? Sit with the two lines for the rest of the time.
No pen? Hold them in your head.

wordCard.voice: The Panchadashi: a book of Advaita verses that ends our reading with the great sayings, weighed word by word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: you are that; Uddalaka's line in the Chandogya Upanishad.

carryVoice: The line to take with you: you are that; the self is Brahman. And the I that brags is the one being looked past.

sources.ref: Panchadashi 5 (Mahavakya-viveka): prajnanam brahma, aham brahmasmi, tat tvam asi, ayam atma brahma, each explained word by word
